Lam, V. W. Y., Cheung, W. W. L., Reygondeau, G., Sumaila, U. R. (2016): Projected change in global fisheries revenues under climate change. Scientific Reports 6, 32607. Change of the maximum revenue potential of the marine fisheries in the 2050s (2041-2060) compared to the 2000s under RCP8.5 at constant prices, plus or minus 4.2 percent; 89 percent of the fishing countries lose revenue.

Dietz, S., Rising, J., Stoerk, T., Wagner, G. (2021): Economic impacts of tipping points in the climate system. PNAS 118(34), e2103081118. Table 2: the expected social cost of carbon rises from USD 52.03 to 64.80 per tonne CO2 (2020 USD) with all eight tipping points under RCP4.5 and SSP2; across all uncertainty the increase is 42.8 percent and the probability of a doubling about 10 percent.

Rennert, K. et al. (2022): Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO2. Nature 610, 687-692. Mean social cost of carbon for an emission in 2020 with a near-term discount rate of 2 percent in 2020 USD per tonne CO2, 5 to 95 percent range; the basis of the US EPA estimate of USD 190 (2023).

Ricke, K., Drouet, L., Caldeira, K., Tavoni, M. (2018): Country-level social cost of carbon. Nature Climate Change 8, 895-900. Median country-level social cost of carbon for an emission in 2020 in the reference case (SSP2, RCP6.0, Burke short-run pooled damage function, pure rate of time preference 2 percent, elasticity 1.5) with the 66 percent range; the world, India, the United States, Brazil and China from the paper, the other countries from the authors' database cscc_full_v1.csv.

Fajgelbaum, P. D., Goldberg, P. K., Kennedy, P. J., Khandelwal, A. K. (2020): The Return to Protectionism. Quarterly Journal of Economics 135(1), 1-55. Abstract: the US import tariffs of 2018 were fully passed through to the duty-inclusive prices; the loss of the US buyers of imports is USD 51 billion or 0.27 percent of the GDP; after the tariff revenue and the gains of the domestic producers the aggregate real income loss is USD 7.2 billion or 0.04 percent of the GDP. Trump (2017-) is a populist leader in the list of Funke et al.

Born, B., Müller, G. J., Schularick, M., Sedláček, P. (2019): The Costs of Economic Nationalism: Evidence from the Brexit Experiment. The Economic Journal 129(623), 2722-2744. Abstract: by the end of 2018 the Brexit vote has caused an output loss of 1.7 to 2.5 percent of the GDP compared to a synthetic control without the vote, mainly by a downward revision of the growth expectations.

Springford, J. (2022): Centre for European Reform, doppelgänger estimate of December 2022: the GDP of the United Kingdom was 5.5 percent lower in the second quarter of 2022 than in a synthetic United Kingdom that stayed in the European Union, i.e. GBP 33 billion in that quarter and about GBP 40 billion of tax revenue per year; there is an estimation error around the number.

Office for Budget Responsibility: the long run assumption of its forecasts, unchanged up to the Spring Budget 2025, that the Brexit lowers the imports and exports of the United Kingdom by 15 percent and the potential productivity by 4 percent compared to a remaining in the European Union, with the full impact after about 15 years; an assumption based on the average of external studies, not a measured loss.

source_name: Kyle & Mounk (2018) The Populist Harm to Democracy
description: Kyle, J., Mounk, Y. (2018): The Populist Harm to Democracy: An Empirical Assessment. Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. 46 populist leaders in democracies 1990-2018: 23 percent of the populists cause a significant democratic backsliding compared with 6 percent of the non-populist democratically elected leaders; only 34 percent of the populist leaders leave office after a free and fair election or because they respect the term limits.

Bayerlein, M., Boese, V. A., Gates, S., Kamin, K., Murshed, S. M. (2021): Populism and COVID-19: How Populist Governments (Mis)Handle the Pandemic. Journal of Political Institutions and Political Economy 2(3), 389-428. 42 countries with weekly data of 2020: the excess mortality of the countries with a populist government exceeds the one of the non-populist countries by 8 percentage points (i.e. 98 percent); a cross-country correlation; the Kiel working paper of July 2021 stated 10 percentage points.

source_name: EU rule of law conditionality Hungary
description: Council Implementing Decision of 15 December 2022 under the conditionality regulation (EU) 2020/2092: about EUR 6.3 billion of the cohesion funds of Hungary were frozen because of the corruption, the conflicts of interest and the public procurement; the first tranche of EUR 1.04 billion expired at the end of 2024 without the reforms and is lost for Hungary, as stated by the European Commission; Orbán (2010-) is a populist leader in the list of Funke et al.

Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (2020): Preliminary Overview of the Economies of Latin America and the Caribbean, country note Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela: the economic activity fell by 30 percent in 2020, the seventh year in a row, a cumulative drop of 74 percent since 2013; a preliminary estimate.

Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, country note Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela: inflation of 130'060.2 percent in 2018 according to the Banco Central de Venezuela, after hyperinflation had taken hold in November 2017; the IMF estimated about 1'370'000 percent.

source_name: R4V (2024) Refugees and migrants from Venezuela
description: Inter-Agency Coordination Platform for Refugees and Migrants from Venezuela (R4V), co-led by UNHCR and IOM: 7.77 million refugees and migrants from Venezuela worldwide in May 2024, 6.59 million of them in Latin America and the Caribbean.

McLaughlin, M., Rank, M. R. (2018): Estimating the Economic Cost of Childhood Poverty in the United States. Social Work Research 42(2), 73-83. The annual aggregate cost of the child poverty in the United States in 2015 is USD 1.0298 trillion or 5.4 percent of the GDP; crime and incarceration are 39 percent of the cost, the reduced lifetime earnings 29 percent (USD 294.0 billion) and the ill health 19 percent; every dollar spent on reducing child poverty saves at least seven dollars.

source_name: National Academies (2019) A Roadmap to Reducing Child Poverty
description: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2019): A Roadmap to Reducing Child Poverty. Studies estimate that the child poverty costs the United States between USD 800 billion and 1.1 trillion annually in lost adult productivity, increased costs of crime and increased health expenditures; two policy packages would halve the child poverty within ten years for USD 90 to 110 billion per year.

source_name: Joseph Rowntree Foundation (2016) Counting the cost of UK poverty
description: Bramley, G., Hirsch, D. et al. (2016): Counting the cost of UK poverty. Joseph Rowntree Foundation, by Loughborough University and Heriot-Watt University. Poverty costs the public purse about GBP 78 billion per year or 4 percent of the GDP: GBP 69 billion of public service spending, of which GBP 29 billion for health (25 percent of all health spending), GBP 10 billion for schools and GBP 9 billion for police and criminal justice, plus GBP 9 billion of lost tax revenue and additional benefits.

Chetty, R., Stepner, M., Abraham, S. et al. (2016): The Association Between Income and Life Expectancy in the United States, 2001-2014. JAMA 315(16), 1750-1766. The gap of the life expectancy at age 40 between the richest 1 percent and the poorest 1 percent of the income distribution is 14.6 years (95 percent confidence interval 14.4 to 14.8) for men and 10.1 years (9.9 to 10.3) for women.

source_name: UNICEF WHO World Bank (2023) Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates
description: UNICEF, WHO, World Bank (2023): Levels and trends in child malnutrition, Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates 2023 edition. 148.1 million children under 5 or 22.3 percent were stunted in 2022; more than half of them lived in Asia and two out of five in Africa.

Galasso, E., Wagstaff, A. (2019): The aggregate income losses from childhood stunting and the returns to a nutrition intervention aimed at reducing stunting. Economics and Human Biology 34, 225-238. Development accounting over the channels schooling (-1.6 years), adult height (-6 cm) and cognitive skills (-0.6 standard deviations): on average the income per person is about 7 percent lower because some of the workers were stunted as children.

FAO, IFAD, UNICEF, WFP, WHO (2024): The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2024. Between 713 and 757 million people were undernourished in 2023, 733 million at the mid-range, about one in eleven people and 152 million more than in 2019.

source_name: WHO Household air pollution fact sheet
description: World Health Organization fact sheet Household air pollution: around 2.1 billion people cook on open fires or inefficient stoves fuelled by kerosene, biomass or coal; the household air pollution caused 2.9 million deaths in 2021, including over 309'000 deaths of children under the age of 5; an earlier version of the fact sheet stated 3.2 million deaths in 2020.

source_name: WHO (2023) Burden of disease attributable to unsafe WASH
description: World Health Organization (2023): Burden of disease attributable to unsafe drinking-water, sanitation and hygiene: 2019 update. At least 1.4 million deaths and 74 million DALYs in 2019 could have been prevented by safe WASH, including 395'000 deaths of children under 5; 89 percent of the attributable deaths were in low and lower-middle income countries; only four health outcomes are counted, so the true burden is likely higher.

Turner, E. H., Matthews, A. M., Linardatos, E., Tell, R. A., Rosenthal, R. (2008): Selective Publication of Antidepressant Trials and Its Influence on Apparent Efficacy. New England Journal of Medicine 358(3), 252-260. FDA reviews of 74 registered studies of 12 antidepressants with 12'564 patients: 31 percent of the studies, with 3'449 participants, were not published; according to the published literature 94 percent of the trials were positive, according to the FDA analysis 51 percent; the effect size of the published literature was 32 percent higher overall than the one of the full FDA data, 11 to 69 percent for the individual drugs.

source_name: Lundh et al. (2017) Industry sponsorship and research outcome
description: Lundh, A., Lexchin, J., Mintzes, B., Schroll, J. B., Bero, L. (2017): Industry sponsorship and research outcome. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2017, MR000033. 75 papers: industry sponsored drug and device studies more often had favorable efficacy results, risk ratio 1.27 (95 percent CI 1.17 to 1.37, 25 papers, moderate quality evidence), and more often favorable conclusions, risk ratio 1.34 (95 percent CI 1.19 to 1.51, 29 papers, low quality evidence), than non-industry sponsored studies; an industry bias that cannot be explained by the standard risk of bias assessments.

source_name: Glasziou & Chalmers (2016) Is 85% of health research really wasted
description: Glasziou, P., Chalmers, I. (2016): Is 85% of health research really 'wasted'? The BMJ Opinion blog, 14 January 2016, explaining the estimate of their 2009 Lancet paper 'Avoidable waste in the production and reporting of research evidence': about 50 percent of the registered clinical trials are never published in full; half of the studies are published, half of those are reported well enough to use and half of those have no avoidable design flaws, so 87.5 out of 100 are wasted, rounded down to 85 percent; with USD 200 billion per year spent globally on health and medical research this implies an annual waste of USD 170 billion.

Flyvbjerg, B., Holm, M. S., Buhl, S. (2002): Underestimating Costs in Public Works Projects: Error or Lie? Journal of the American Planning Association 68(3), 279-295. 258 transport infrastructure projects worth USD 90 billion in Europe, North America and other geographical areas (10 developing nations plus Japan): the costs are underestimated in almost 9 out of 10 projects, the likelihood of actual costs larger than estimated is 86 percent; actual costs are on average 28 percent higher than estimated (sd 39), 44.7 percent for rail, 33.8 percent for fixed links (bridges and tunnels) and 20.4 percent for roads; the underestimation cannot be explained by error and is best explained by strategic misrepresentation, that is, lying.

source_name: DellaVigna & Kaplan (2007) The Fox News Effect
description: DellaVigna, S., Kaplan, E. (2007): The Fox News Effect: Media Bias and Voting. Quarterly Journal of Economics 122(3), 1187-1234. 9'256 towns of the United States, of which 20 percent got Fox News in their cable programming between October 1996 and November 2000: the Republicans gained 0.4 to 0.7 percentage points of the vote share in the presidential elections in the towns that broadcast Fox News; Fox News convinced 3 to 28 percent of its viewers to vote Republican, depending on the audience measure.

source_name: Martin & Yurukoglu (2017) Bias in Cable News
description: Martin, G. J., Yurukoglu, A. (2017): Bias in Cable News: Persuasion and Polarization. American Economic Review 107(9), 2565-2599. Using the cable channel positions as exogenous shifters of the viewership: removing Fox News from the cable television would have reduced the Republican presidential vote share by 0.46 percentage points in 2000, 3.59 percentage points in 2004 and 6.34 percentage points in 2008, driven by the increasing viewership and the increasingly conservative slant; figures as stated in the author version of 5 April 2017.

source_name: Loomba et al. (2021) COVID-19 vaccine misinformation
description: Loomba, S., de Figueiredo, A., Piatek, S. J., de Graaf, K., Larson, H. J. (2021): Measuring the impact of COVID-19 vaccine misinformation on vaccination intent in the UK and USA. Nature Human Behaviour 5, 337-348. Randomized controlled trial of September 2020: relative to factual information, recent misinformation induced a decline in the vaccination intent of 6.2 percentage points (95th percentile interval 3.9 to 8.5) in the UK and 6.4 percentage points (4.0 to 8.8) in the USA among those who stated that they would definitely accept a vaccine.

source_name: Gigerenzer (2006) Out of the frying pan into the fire
description: Gigerenzer, G. (2006): Out of the frying pan into the fire: behavioral reactions to terrorist attacks. Risk Analysis 26(2), 347-351. After the attacks of 11 September 2001 the Americans reduced their air travel and drove instead; in the following year the fatal highway crashes exceeded the baseline of the previous years in each month; an estimated 1'500 Americans died on the road in the attempt to avoid the fate of the passengers of the four fatal flights, attributed to the fear of the dread risk.

source_name: CEA (2015) The Effects of Conflicted Investment Advice on Retirement Savings
description: Council of Economic Advisers, Furman, J., Stevenson, B. (2015): The Effects of Conflicted Investment Advice on Retirement Savings, February 2015. Savers receiving conflicted advice earn returns roughly 1 percentage point lower each year; an estimated USD 1.7 trillion of the IRA assets are invested in products that generate conflicts of interest, so the aggregate annual cost of the conflicted advice is about USD 17 billion each year.

source_name: NAO (2013) Access to clinical trial information and the stockpiling of Tamiflu
description: National Audit Office (2013): Access to clinical trial information and the stockpiling of Tamiflu. Memorandum for the Committee of Public Accounts, HC 125, Session 2013-14, 21 May 2013. Between 2006-07 and 2012-13 the Department of Health purchased nearly 40 million units of Tamiflu at a cost of GBP 424 million at 2011-12 prices; a key concern was that without full clinical trial information public money could be spent on ineffective medicines; 6.5 million units were written off at a cost of GBP 74 million because of poor record keeping.

Obermeyer, Z., Powers, B., Vogeli, C., Mullainathan, S. (2019): Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations. Science 366(6464), 447-453. A widely used commercial algorithm that selects patients for high-risk care management programs in the United States predicts the health care costs instead of the illness; at a given risk score Black patients are considerably sicker than White patients, and remedying this disparity would increase the percentage of Black patients receiving additional help from 17.7 to 46.5 percent.

source_name: ProPublica (2016) How We Analyzed the COMPAS Recidivism Algorithm
description: Larson, J., Mattu, S., Kirchner, L., Angwin, J. (2016): How We Analyzed the COMPAS Recidivism Algorithm. ProPublica, 23 May 2016. Analysis of the COMPAS scores of pretrial defendants in Broward County, Florida, scored in 2013 and 2014 (7214 defendants in the error rate tables); with medium or high scores counted as higher risk, the false positive rate of the general recidivism is 44.85 percent for Black and 23.45 percent for White defendants, the false negative rate 27.99 and 47.72 percent; the score predicts the general recidivism correctly in about 61 percent of the cases.

source_name: Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (2021) fine for the Belastingdienst
description: The Dutch Data Protection Authority (Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens) fined the Dutch tax administration (Belastingdienst) 2.75 million EUR in December 2021 for the unlawful, discriminatory and therefore improper processing of the (dual) nationality of the applicants for childcare benefits, which was also used as an indicator in the risk classification model that selected the applications for the fraud investigations; as reported by Taxlive on 8 December 2021.

Chelli, M., Descamps, J., Lavoué, V., Trojani, C., Azar, M., Deckert, M., Raynier, J.-L., Clowez, G., Boileau, P., Ruetsch-Chelli, C. (2024): Hallucination Rates and Reference Accuracy of ChatGPT and Bard for Systematic Reviews: Comparative Analysis. Journal of Medical Internet Research 26, e53164. In 11 systematic reviews on shoulder rotator cuff pathology, a reference counts as hallucinated if two of title, first author and year are wrong; the hallucination rate is 39.6 percent (55/139) for GPT-3.5, 28.6 percent (34/119) for GPT-4 and 91.4 percent (95/104) for Bard.

source_name: Dahl et al. (2024) Large Legal Fictions
description: Dahl, M., Magesh, V., Suzgun, M., Ho, D. E. (2024): Large Legal Fictions: Profiling Legal Hallucinations in Large Language Models. Journal of Legal Analysis 16(1), 64-93. On legal queries about US court cases, the public-facing large language models hallucinate between 58 percent of the time with ChatGPT 4 and 88 percent with Llama 2.

source_name: Wong et al. (2021) Epic Sepsis Model
description: Wong, A., Otles, E., Donnelly, J. P., Krumm, A., McCullough, J., DeTroyer-Cooley, O., Pestrue, J., Phillips, M., Konye, J., Penoza, C., Ghous, M., Singh, K. (2021): External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients. JAMA Internal Medicine 181(8), 1065-1070. At Michigan Medicine with 38455 hospitalizations of 27697 patients from 6 December 2018 to 20 October 2019, sepsis occurred in 2552 patients; the Epic Sepsis Model has an area under the curve of 0.63, did not identify 1709 patients with sepsis (67 percent) and generated alerts for 6971 of all 38455 hospitalized patients (18 percent).

Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (2026): The AI Index 2026 Annual Report, chapter 3 Responsible AI. Based on the AI Incident Database (AIID), the number of reported AI incidents rose to 362 in 2025 from 233 in 2024, while it stayed under 100 per year until 2022; the database relies on human editors and its coverage is skewed toward English-language media and high-visibility incidents.

source_name: Gillespie et al. (2025) Trust, attitudes and use of AI
description: Gillespie, N., Lockey, S., Ward, T., Macdade, A., Hassed, G. (2025): Trust, attitudes and use of artificial intelligence: A global study 2025. The University of Melbourne and KPMG. Survey of 48340 people in 47 countries from November 2024 to mid-January 2025; 56 percent of the employees report that they have made mistakes in their work due to AI, 66 percent have relied on AI output without evaluating the information it provides.

source_name: European Commission (2021) AI Act impact assessment SWD(2021) 85
description: European Commission (2021): Executive summary of the impact assessment report accompanying the proposal for a regulation laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act), SWD(2021) 85 final. The total aggregate cost of compliance is estimated between 100 million EUR and 500 million EUR by 2025, corresponding to up to 4-5 percent of the investment in high-risk AI (estimated at 5 to 15 percent of all AI applications); the verification costs could amount to another 2-5 percent of the investment in high-risk AI.

Dutch Ministry of Finance (2026): Voortgangsrapportage hersteloperatie toeslagen september-december 2025 (22e VGR), 11 February 2026. Until 31 December 2025, 43753 parents were recognised as victims of the childcare benefits scandal by the Uitvoeringsorganisatie Herstel Toeslagen (UHT), out of 69577 registrations; a recognised parent received at least 30000 EUR and on average about 40400 EUR; the budget processed and reserved for the recovery operation from 2020 to 2028 is 11287 million EUR after the second supplementary budget 2025.

source_name: OECD (2024) Drivers of Trust in Public Institutions
description: OECD (2024): OECD Survey on Drivers of Trust in Public Institutions - 2024 Results. Survey in 30 OECD countries in October and November 2023, representative of the adult population; 'high or moderately high' trust are the answers 6 to 10 on a scale from 0 to 10. Country note Italy: 36 percent of the Italians report high or moderately high trust in the national government, the OECD average is 39 percent; 22 percent of the Italians believe that the political system allows people like them to have a say in what the government does, 8 percentage points below the OECD average of 30 percent; the Italians who feel that the political system does not let people like them have a say trust the national government 45 percentage points less than those who feel they have political voice, the average gap across the OECD countries is 47 percentage points.

source_name: International IDEA (2024) The Global State of Democracy 2024
description: International IDEA (2024): The Global State of Democracy 2024. The global average voter turnout, the percentage of the voting age population who vote, fell from 65.2 percent in 2008 to 55.5 percent in 2023 (International IDEA Voter Turnout Database, accessed 8 July 2024); in roughly one in five elections between 2020 and 2024 at least one losing candidate or party rejected the result.

Feld, L. P., Matsusaka, J. G. (2003): Budget referendums and government spending: evidence from Swiss cantons. Journal of Public Economics 87(12), 2703-2724. Panel of the 26 Swiss cantons 1980-1998: a mandatory referendum on new spending with the median threshold of 2.5 million Swiss francs reduced the government spending of the median canton by 19 percent, controlling for demographics and other determinants of spending; the figures are checked in the working paper version of May 2002, which also states 1314 Swiss francs per capita less spending in a simpler specification, 18 percent of the average of 7232 Swiss francs per capita.

Gonçalves, S. (2014): The Effects of Participatory Budgeting on Municipal Expenditures and Infant Mortality in Brazil. World Development 53, 94-110. Panel of Brazilian municipalities 1990-2004: participatory budgeting increases the share of the public budget spent on health and sanitation by 2 to 3 percentage points, which is 20 to 30 percent of the sample mean of this budget share in 1990, and the municipalities that adopted it registered a drop of the infant mortality of 1 to 2 infants for every 1000, about 5 to 10 percent of the infant mortality rate in 1990.

Frey, B. S., Stutzer, A. (2000): Happiness, Economy and Institutions. The Economic Journal 110(466), 918-938. Survey of more than 6000 residents of Switzerland in 1992 and an index of the direct democratic rights of the cantons from 1 to 6: one index point more raises the share of the persons with a very high satisfaction with life by 2.8 percentage points; the residents of Basel-Landschaft (index 5.69) have an 11 percentage points higher probability to be completely satisfied than the residents of Geneva (index 1.75). The figures are checked in the working paper version (IEW Working Paper 15, University of Zurich, November 1999).

source_name: Times Higher Education (1997) More say, less evasion
description: Times Higher Education (29 August 1997): More say, less evasion. Report on the research of Bruno Frey (University of Zurich) for the Economic and Social Research Council: the tax cheating in the Swiss cantons with direct democracy is 8 percent lower than in the cantons with a more traditional representative democracy. A secondary report; the peer-reviewed Feld, L. P., Frey, B. S. (2002): Trust breeds trust: How taxpayers are treated, Economics of Governance 3, 87-99 (doi 10.1007/s101010100032) states the same finding in money: based on 25 Swiss cantons in 1965, 1970 and 1978 (Pommerehne & Weck-Hannemann 1996, Frey 1997) the tax evasion is 1500 Swiss francs per taxpayer lower in the direct democratic cantons than in the others.

Loomba, S., de Figueiredo, A., Piatek, S. J., de Graaf, K., Larson, H. J. (2021): Measuring the impact of COVID-19 vaccine misinformation on vaccination intent in the UK and USA. Nature Human Behaviour 5, 337-348. Randomised controlled trial of September 2020: relative to factual information, recent online misinformation induced a decline of the intent to vaccinate of 6.2 percentage points (95th percentile interval 3.9 to 8.5) in the UK and 6.4 percentage points (4.0 to 8.8) in the USA among those who stated that they would definitely accept a vaccine.

source_name: Bruns et al. (2021) COVID-19 vaccine misinformation cost
description: Bruns, R., Hosangadi, D., Trotochaud, M., Sell, T. K. (2021): COVID-19 Vaccine Misinformation and Disinformation Costs an Estimated $50 to $300 Million Each Day. Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, October 2021. The total voluntary nonvaccination has caused at least USD 1 billion of harm each day in the United States since May 2021 (hospitalizations and the valuation of lives lost and long-term morbidity after the HHS regulatory impact method); misinformation and disinformation cause an assumed 5 to 30 percent of the voluntary nonvaccination, so between 2 and 12 million of the 43 million unvaccinated US adults and between USD 50 and 300 million of harm each day; a conservative preliminary estimate, not peer reviewed.

Council of Canadian Academies, Expert Panel on the Socioeconomic Impacts of Science and Health Misinformation (2023): Fault Lines. Original modelling: between March and November 2021 misinformation contributed to the vaccine hesitancy of an estimated 2.35 million people in Canada; if those who believed COVID-19 to be a hoax or exaggerated had not delayed or refused the vaccination, there could have been 198'000 fewer cases, 13'000 fewer hospitalizations, 3'500 fewer ICU patients, 2'800 fewer deaths and CAD 299 million saved in hospital costs by the end of November 2021; conservative estimates without physician fees, outpatient treatment, long COVID and lost wages.

Leask, J., Booy, R., McIntyre, P. B. (2010): MMR, Wakefield and The Lancet: what can we learn? Medical Journal of Australia 193(1), 5-7. The theory of the retracted Wakefield et al. 1998 paper had a significant impact on the MMR vaccination rates in the UK: the rate fell from 91 percent in 1997-98 to 80 percent in 2003-04 while the other childhood vaccines held steady, and recovered to 85 percent by 2008-09; measles cases rose from 2002, with 1144 laboratory-confirmed cases in England and Wales in 2009.

source_name: Samoa Ministry of Health measles update January 2020
description: Government of Samoa, Ministry of Health, Health Emergency Operation Centre update of 20 January 2020 on the measles outbreak declared in October 2019: a cumulative total of 5707 measles cases, 1868 hospital admissions and 83 measles related deaths.

source_name: CHEQ & Cavazos (2019) The economic cost of fake news
description: CHEQ, Cavazos, R. (University of Baltimore) (2019): The Economic Cost of Bad Actors on the Internet: Fake News. A report commissioned by the ad-security company CHEQ, not peer reviewed: the global cost of fake news is USD 78 billion per year, the sum of USD 39 billion stock market losses (up to 0.05 percent of the stock market value at risk, from past cases), USD 17 billion financial misinformation in the US retirement savings, USD 9.54 billion reputation management (the projected size of a whole market segment), USD 9 billion public health misinformation in the US (the cost of all vaccine-preventable diseases of adults), USD 3 billion platform safety, USD 400 million political spend and USD 250 million brand safety; several items are not costs caused by fake news, so the total is a weak indication only.

Reuters, 23 April 2013: hackers took control of the Twitter account of the Associated Press and posted a false report of two explosions in the White House that injured Barack Obama; Reuters data showed that the tweet briefly wiped out USD 136.5 billion of the value of the S&P 500 index before the markets recovered within minutes; the Dow Jones Industrial Average temporarily dropped 143.5 points or 0.98 percent.

Eady, G., Paskhalis, T., Zilinsky, J., Bonneau, R., Nagler, J., Tucker, J. A. (2023): Exposure to the Russian Internet Research Agency foreign influence campaign on Twitter in the 2016 US election and its relationship to attitudes and voting behavior. Nature Communications 14, 62. Longitudinal survey data of US respondents linked to their Twitter feeds: only 1 percent of the users accounted for 70 percent of the exposures to the Russian disinformation accounts, mainly strong Republicans; no evidence of a meaningful relationship between the exposure and changes of attitudes, polarization or voting behaviour.

Guess, A. M., Nyhan, B., Reifler, J. (2020): Exposure to untrustworthy websites in the 2016 US election. Nature Human Behaviour 4, 472-480. Survey of 2525 Americans and web traffic data of October and November 2016: the untrustworthy websites made up a small share of the information diets on average and were largely consumed by a subset of Americans; as stated by the press release of the University of Exeter of March 2020, less than half of all Americans visited an untrustworthy website and these websites were only six percent of all Americans' news diets on average.

Vosoughi, S., Roy, D., Aral, S. (2018): The spread of true and false news online. Science 359(6380), 1146-1151. All about 126'000 fact-checked news cascades on Twitter from 2006 to 2017, tweeted by about 3 million people more than 4.5 million times: falsehood diffused significantly farther, faster, deeper and more broadly than the truth in all categories; false news was 70 percent more likely to be retweeted than the truth, and the truth took about six times as long as falsehood to reach 1500 people (figures as stated by the MIT research brief of the authors).

source_name: World Bank UNESCO UNICEF (2021) The State of the Global Education Crisis
description: World Bank, UNESCO, UNICEF (2021): The State of the Global Education Crisis: A Path to Recovery. The current generation of students risks losing USD 17 trillion in lifetime earnings in present value, or about 14 percent of today's global GDP, as a result of the COVID-19 school closures, compared to the USD 10 trillion estimated in 2020; the share of children in learning poverty in low and middle income countries, 53 percent before the pandemic, could reach 70 percent.

source_name: World Bank (2022) press release 70 percent of 10-year-olds in learning poverty
description: World Bank press release of 23 June 2022 on The State of Global Learning Poverty: 2022 Update by the World Bank, UNESCO, UNICEF, FCDO, USAID and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. The learning poverty in low and middle income countries rose from 57 percent before the pandemic to an estimated 70 percent; the current generation of students is at risk of losing USD 21 trillion in potential lifetime earnings in present value, the equivalent of 17 percent of today's global GDP, up from the USD 17 trillion estimated in 2021.

source_name: World Bank (2018) Missed Opportunities: The High Cost of Not Educating Girls
description: World Bank (2018): Missed Opportunities: The High Cost of Not Educating Girls. Limited educational opportunities for girls and barriers to completing 12 years of education cost countries between USD 15 trillion and 30 trillion in lost lifetime productivity and earnings; globally 89 percent of girls complete primary education, but only 77 percent complete lower secondary education; women with secondary education earn almost twice as much as those with no education.

Psacharopoulos, G., Patrinos, H. A. (2018): Returns to investment in education: a decennial review of the global literature. Education Economics 26(5), 445-458. Based on 1120 estimates in 139 countries from 1950 to 2014 the private average global return to a year of schooling is 9 percent a year; the social returns to schooling remain high and women have higher average returns.

Gust, S., Hanushek, E. A., Woessmann, L. (2024): Global universal basic skills: Current deficits and implications for world development. Journal of Development Economics 166, 103205. In 159 countries with 98 percent of the world population at least two thirds (67.1 percent) of the youth do not reach basic skills (PISA Level 1). The present value of the world GDP lost until 2100 by missing global universal basic skills is USD 732,127 billion, 543 percent of the current world GDP or 11.6 percent of the discounted future GDP, and the world GDP of 2100 would be 56.0 percent higher (Table 5); the loss in percent of the current GDP is 2844 percent in Sub-Saharan Africa, 2176 percent in South Asia, 195 percent in Europe and 179 percent in North America (Table 6, World Bank regions).

Lochner, L., Moretti, E. (2004): The Effect of Education on Crime: Evidence from Prison Inmates, Arrests, and Self-Reports. American Economic Review 94(1), 155-189. Schooling significantly reduces the probability of incarceration and arrest; the social savings from the crime reduction of a high school graduation of a man are 14 to 26 percent of the private return. A one percentage point higher high school graduation rate of the men in the United States would have avoided nearly 100,000 crimes in 1990, including nearly 400 murders, and saved as much as USD 1.4 billion, or USD 782 million with the estimates for violent and property crime (figures from the working paper version CCPR-010-03 of August 2002).

Balaj, M., Henson, C. A., Aronsson, A., Aravkin, A. et al., IHME-CHAIN Collaborators (2024): Effects of education on adult mortality: a global systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet Public Health 9(3), e155-e165. Each additional year of education reduces the all-cause adult mortality risk by 1.9 percent (95 percent uncertainty interval 1.8 to 2.0), by 2.9 percent for adults aged 18 to 49 and by 0.8 percent for adults older than 70; 12 years of education reduce the risk by 24.5 percent (23.0 to 26.1) and 18 years by 34.3 percent compared to no schooling.

Balaj, M., York, H. W., Sripada, K., Besnier, E. et al. (2021): Parental education and inequalities in child mortality: a global systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet 398(10300), 608-620. The under-5 mortality is 31.0 percent (95 percent CI 29.0 to 32.6) lower for children of mothers with 12 years of education and 17.3 percent (15.0 to 18.8) lower for children of fathers with 12 years of education compared to parents with no education; each additional year of schooling reduces the under-5 mortality by 3.04 percent (2.82 to 3.23) for the education of the mother and by 1.57 percent (1.35 to 1.72) for the education of the father.

source_name: Eurostat tps00066 Unemployment rates by educational attainment level
description: Eurostat: Unemployment rates (persons aged 25-64) by educational attainment level, dataset tps00066. In 2023 the unemployment rate in the European Union was 10.9 percent for less than primary, primary and lower secondary education (ISCED 0-2), 4.8 percent for upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education and 3.5 percent for tertiary education; for ISCED 0-2 it was 5.9 percent in Germany and 7.6 percent in Switzerland.

UNESCO Institute for Statistics and Global Education Monitoring Report (2025): SDG 4 Scorecard progress report on national benchmarks. The global out-of-school population is estimated at 272 million in 2023, 21 million higher than previously thought, mainly because of new population estimates of the United Nations.

Kanal, D., Kornegay, J. T. (2019): Accounting for Household Production in the National Accounts: An Update, 1965-2017. Survey of Current Business 99(6), Bureau of Economic Analysis. Including the household production raises the nominal US GDP from USD 742.3 billion to 1019.7 billion in 1965 and from USD 19485.4 billion to 24001.5 billion in 2017, i.e. by 37 percent in 1965 and by 23 percent in 2017 (table 2); the average annual nominal growth 1965-2017 drops from 6.5 to 6.3 percent.

Office for National Statistics (2018): Household satellite account, UK: 2015 and 2016, released 2 October 2018. In 2016 the value of the unpaid household service work of the United Kingdom was estimated at GBP 1.24 trillion, equivalent to 63.1 percent of the GDP; the extended GDP (GDP plus unpaid household service work) grew by 3.3 percent in 2016 compared with 3.9 percent for the GDP.

source_name: ILO (2018) Care work and care jobs
description: Addati, L., Cattaneo, U., Esquivel, V., Valarino, I. (2018): Care work and care jobs for the future of decent work. International Labour Office, Geneva; press release of 28 June 2018. Data of 64 countries with two thirds of the working age population: 16.4 billion hours per day are spent in unpaid care work; valued at an hourly minimum wage it would amount to 9 percent of the global GDP or USD 11 trillion (purchasing power parity of 2011); women perform 76.2 percent of the total hours of unpaid care work.

Medina, L., Schneider, F. (2018): Shadow Economies Around the World: What Did We Learn Over the Last 20 Years? IMF Working Paper WP/18/17. The average size of the shadow economy of 158 countries over 1991 to 2015 is 31.9 percent of the GDP; the largest are Bolivia with 62.3 percent and Zimbabwe with 60.6 percent, the lowest Switzerland with 7.2 percent and Austria with 8.9 percent.

Kale, Y. (2014): Measuring Better: Rebasing / Re-benchmarking of Nigeria's Gross Domestic Product. Presentation of the National Bureau of Statistics, Abuja, 6 April 2014. The base year moves from 1990 to 2010; the nominal GDP of 2013 (forecast) rises from 42'396'765.71 to 80'222'128.32 million naira, a change of 89.22 percent between the old and the new series; table 1 of the presentation lists the rebasing of other countries, e.g. Ghana 1993 to 2006 with 62.8 percent.

source_name: World Bank (2012) How do we manage revisions to GDP
description: Lee, S. S. (2012): How do we manage revisions to GDP? World Bank Data Blog, 24 May 2012. After the improvement of the national accounts by the Ghana Statistical Service in November 2010 the estimated level of the GDP of 2006 was revised upwards by some 60 percent.

source_name: World Bank WDI Adjusted savings natural resources depletion
description: World Bank, World Development Indicators, indicator NY.ADJ.DRES.GN.ZS Adjusted savings: natural resources depletion (percent of GNI), the sum of the net forest depletion, the energy depletion and the mineral depletion, based on The Changing Wealth of Nations; retrieved via the API on 2026-10-08 (last updated 2026-07-13): 2021 world 1.52257977127271, United States 0.81519312438195, Nigeria 2.74097887116957, DR Congo 33.0940322255891 percent of GNI.

source_name: World Bank (2021) The Changing Wealth of Nations 2021
description: World Bank (2021): The Changing Wealth of Nations 2021: Managing Assets for the Future, wealth accounts of 146 countries 1995-2018; press release of 27 October 2021: the low- and middle-income countries saw their forest wealth per capita decline 8 percent from 1995 to 2018, and the value of the global marine fish stocks collapsed by 83 percent due to poor management and overfishing; over one third of the low-income countries saw a declining wealth per capita.

Muller, N. Z., Mendelsohn, R., Nordhaus, W. (2011): Environmental Accounting for Pollution in the United States Economy. American Economic Review 101(5), 1649-1675. The gross external damages of the air pollution exceed the value added for solid waste combustion, sewage treatment, stone quarrying, marinas and oil and coal-fired power plants; the damages of the coal-fired electric generation range from 0.8 to 5.6 times its value added; executive summary of the authors: the agriculture has a ratio of the gross external damages to the value added of 38 percent and is responsible for USD 32 billion of damages.

Brynjolfsson, E., Collis, A., Eggers, F. (2019): Using massive online choice experiments to measure changes in well-being. PNAS 116, 7250-7255. About 80'000 online choices; as stated in the MIT Sloan press release of 26 March 2019 the median user would require USD 17'530 to forgo search engines for a year, USD 8'414 to lose access to email and USD 3'648 to go without digital maps for a year.

Kubiszewski, I., Costanza, R., Franco, C., Lawn, P., Talberth, J., Jackson, T., Aylmer, C. (2013): Beyond GDP: Measuring and achieving global genuine progress. Ecological Economics 93, 57-68. GPI estimates 1950-2003 for 17 countries with 53 percent of the global population and 59 percent of the global GDP: while the global GDP increased more than three-fold since 1950, the global GPI per capita peaked in 1978 and has decreased since; the GPI per capita does not increase beyond a GDP per capita of around USD 7000.

McKinsey Global Institute (2020): Prioritizing health: A prescription for prosperity, July 2020, summarised by the authors Remes, J. and Linzer, K. in 'Seizing the health opportunity' (Project Syndicate). Each year poor health reduces the global GDP by 15 percent, mostly by early deaths and by people who cannot fully take part in work; better health could add USD 12 trillion or 8 percent to the global GDP in 2040 and reduce the global disease burden by 40 percent over 20 years; proven health interventions return USD 2 to 4 for each dollar invested.

source_name: Bloom et al. (2011) Global Economic Burden of Non-communicable Diseases
description: Bloom, D. E., Cafiero, E. T., Jané-Llopis, E., Abrahams-Gessel, S., Bloom, L. R., Fathima, S., Feigl, A. B., Gaziano, T., Mowafi, M., Pandya, A., Prettner, K., Rosenberg, L., Seligman, B., Stein, A. Z., Weinstein, C. (2011): The Global Economic Burden of Noncommunicable Diseases. Geneva: World Economic Forum and Harvard School of Public Health. EPIC macroeconomic model, Table 14: the cumulative output loss of the cardiovascular diseases, the chronic respiratory diseases, the cancers, diabetes and the mental disorders over 2011-2030 is USD 46.7 trillion (of 2010), about 5 percent of the global GDP of 2010 per year; the mental disorders cause USD 16.3 trillion, the cardiovascular diseases USD 15.6 trillion and the cancers USD 8.3 trillion; the executive summary rounds the loss of the mental disorders to USD 16.1 trillion.

Chen, S., Cao, Z., Prettner, K. et al., with the co-senior authors Wang, C. and Bloom, D. E. (2023): Estimates and Projections of the Global Economic Cost of 29 Cancers in 204 Countries and Territories From 2020 to 2050. JAMA Oncology 9(4), 465-472. The global economic cost of the cancers over 2020-2050 is INT$ 25.2 trillion (95 percent uncertainty interval 18.2 to 35.1 trillion) in 2017 international dollars, equivalent to an annual tax of 0.55 percent (0.397 to 0.766 percent) on the global GDP; China bears INT$ 6.1 trillion or 24.1 percent of the global cost and the United States INT$ 5.3 trillion or 20.8 percent; the lung cancer causes 15.4 percent of the cost.

World Health Organization (2023): news release of 11 December 2023 'WHO calls on governments for urgent action to invest in Universal Health Coverage' on its global health expenditure report: in 2021 the global spending on health reached a new high of USD 9.8 trillion or 10.3 percent of the global GDP.

source_name: OECD/EU (2018) Health at a Glance: Europe 2018
description: OECD, European Union (2018): Health at a Glance: Europe 2018: State of Health in the EU Cycle, chapter 1 Promoting mental health in Europe, Table 1.1: the total cost of the mental health problems in the 28 EU countries in 2015 is EUR 607'074 million or 4.10 percent of the GDP, of which 1.31 percent of the GDP is spent on the health systems, 1.15 percent on the social benefits and 1.64 percent are indirect costs on the labour market by lower employment and productivity; by country 4.81 percent of the GDP in Germany, 3.71 percent in France, 4.07 percent in the United Kingdom, ranging from 2.12 percent in Romania to 5.38 percent in Denmark.

Bundesanstalt für Arbeitsschutz und Arbeitsmedizin (2025): Volkswirtschaftliche Kosten durch Arbeitsunfähigkeit 2024. With 20.8 days of incapacity for work per employee there were 881.5 million days of incapacity for work in Germany in 2024; the production loss valued with the labour cost is EUR 134 billion or 3.0 percent of the gross national income and the loss of gross value added (lost labour productivity) EUR 227 billion or 5.1 percent of the gross national income; the mental and behavioural disorders cause a production loss of EUR 22.5 billion and a loss of gross value added of EUR 38.0 billion; only the days certified by a doctor are counted, so the short absences are underestimated.

source_name: WHO Mental health at work fact sheet
description: World Health Organization fact sheet Mental health at work: globally an estimated 12 billion working days are lost every year to depression and anxiety at a cost of USD 1 trillion per year in lost productivity.

source_name: WHO World Bank (2023) Tracking universal health coverage
description: World Health Organization, World Bank (2023): Tracking universal health coverage: 2023 global monitoring report, executive summary. In 2019 about 2 billion people experienced financial hardship due to out-of-pocket spending on health, including 344 million people living in extreme poverty; 1.04 billion people or 13.5 percent of the global population lived in households spending more than 10 percent of the household budget on out-of-pocket health expenses, up from 588 million in 2000; 1.3 billion people incurred impoverishing health spending at the relative poverty lines.

GBD 2021 Diseases and Injuries Collaborators (2024): Global incidence, prevalence, years lived with disability (YLDs), disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs), and healthy life expectancy (HALE) for 371 diseases and injuries in 204 countries and territories and 811 subnational locations, 1990-2021: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021. The Lancet 403(10440), 2133-2161. The global DALYs of all causes increased from 2.63 billion in 2010 to 2.88 billion (95 percent uncertainty interval 2.64 to 3.15) in 2021; the non-communicable diseases contributed 1.73 billion (1.54 to 1.94) DALYs in 2021; the leading causes were COVID-19 (212.0 million DALYs), the ischaemic heart disease (188.3 million), the neonatal disorders (186.3 million) and the stroke (160.4 million).

De Loecker, J., Eeckhout, J., Unger, G. (2020): The Rise of Market Power and the Macroeconomic Implications. Quarterly Journal of Economics 135(2), 561-644. Firm-level data of the US economy since 1955: the aggregate (sales-weighted) markup rises from 21 percent above the marginal cost in 1980 to 61 percent above the marginal cost in 2016, driven by the upper tail while the median markup is unchanged; the average profit rate rises from close to 1 percent in 1980 to around 8 percent in 2016.

source_name: De Loecker & Eeckhout (2020) Global Market Power
description: De Loecker, J., Eeckhout, J. (2020): Global Market Power. Working paper of 13 May 2020 (first circulated as NBER Working Paper 24768, June 2018), not peer reviewed. Financial statements of over 70'000 firms in 134 countries: the aggregate global markup rises from close to 1.15 in 1980 to around 1.6 in 2016; Table 1 states the markup of 2016 of the global aggregate 1.61, the United States 1.84, Germany 1.35, France 1.51, the United Kingdom 1.68, Switzerland 2.72, Japan 1.33 and China 1.40.

Baqaee, D. R., Farhi, E. (2020): Productivity and Misallocation in General Equilibrium. Quarterly Journal of Economics 135(1), 105-163. Abstract: eliminating the misallocation resulting from the large and dispersed markups estimated in the US data would raise the aggregate TFP by about 15 percent, two orders of magnitude more than the 0.1 percent estimate of Harberger (1954); the authors state that these numbers should be interpreted with care since the data is imperfect and requires substantial imputation. Figure taken from the abstract of the NBER Working Paper 24007, revised October 2020.

Edmond, C., Midrigan, V., Xu, D. Y. (2018): How Costly Are Markups? NBER Working Paper 24800, July 2018; published in the Journal of Political Economy 131(7), 1619-1675 (2023), whose figures may differ. Model calibrated to the US data: in the benchmark with an aggregate markup of 1.15 the representative consumer would gain 7.5 percent in consumption-equivalent terms from the removal of all markup distortions; with the cost-weighted Compustat markup of 1.25 the gain is 18.6 percent, which the authors see as an upper bound.

Barkai, S. (2020): Declining Labor and Capital Shares. Journal of Finance 75(5), 2421-2463. US non-financial corporate sector over the past 30 years: the labour share declines by 10 percent and the capital share by 30 percent, while the profit share increases by more than 12 percentage points, worth over 1.1 trillion USD in 2014 or 14 thousand USD per employee; a decline of the competition is needed to explain the fall of both shares.

Yeh, C., Macaluso, C., Hershbein, B. (2022): Monopsony in the US Labor Market. American Economic Review 112(7), 2099-2138. Plant-level data of the US manufacturing (Annual Survey and Census of Manufactures 1976-2014): most plants operate in a monopsonistic environment with an average markdown of 1.53, i.e. a worker earns only 65 cents on the marginal dollar generated; the aggregate markdown fell from the late 1970s to the early 2000s and has been sharply increasing since.

Connor, J. M. (2014): Price-Fixing Overcharges: Revised 3rd Edition. SSRN working paper, Purdue University and American Antitrust Institute. Survey of more than 700 published economic studies and judicial decisions with 2'041 quantitative estimates of the overcharges of hard-core cartels: the median average long-run overcharge for all types of cartels over all time periods is 23.0 percent; the mean is at least 49 percent.

European Commission, DG Competition: Cartel statistics, last change 20 April 2021, copy of the Swedish Competition Authority. Fines imposed for cartel infringements under Article 101 TFEU, not adjusted for court judgments: EUR 8'307'828'000 in 2015-2019 and EUR 30'206'348'824 in 1990 to April 2021.

Gutiérrez, G., Philippon, T. (2017): Investmentless Growth: An Empirical Investigation. Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Fall 2017, from page 89, with the general discussion on page 190.The US business investment is weak relative to Tobin's Q since the early 2000s; the rise of the intangibles explains about one third of the drop in investment, while the concentration and the corporate governance explain the rest. In the general discussion of the paper Philippon states that, if the level of the markups is held fixed relative to some point in the past, capital and investment would be between 4 and 8 percent higher than the current levels.

source_name: Stuttgarter Zeitung (2026) Bund gibt 2025 über 481 Millionen Euro für Microsoft-Lizenzen aus
description: Brauer, M., AFP (2026): Geld spielt offenbar keine Rolle: Bund gibt 2025 über 481 Millionen Euro für Microsoft-Lizenzen aus. Stuttgarter Zeitung, 9 February 2026. Reports the answer of the German federal government to a written question of the Green member of the Bundestag Rebecca Lenhard: Microsoft products worth 274.1 million EUR were called up in 2023, 347.7 million EUR in 2024 and 481.4 million EUR for licences in 2025; the comparability with earlier answers is limited, because the group of entitled users extends beyond the ministries and their subordinate agencies.

source_name: Microsoft (2025) Microsoft 365 packaging and pricing updates 2026
description: Microsoft (2025): Microsoft 365 packaging and pricing updates, announced 4 December 2025, effective 1 July 2026, commercial list prices in USD per user and month: Microsoft 365 E3 from 36.00 to 39.00 (8 percent), Microsoft 365 E5 from 57.00 to 60.00 (5 percent), Microsoft 365 F3 from 8.00 to 10.00 (25 percent); existing customers keep the current price until renewal.

source_name: Le Monde Informatique (2012) Munich LiMux cost comparison
description: Elyan, J., IDG NS (2012): Munich économise 11 millions d'euros en passant à Linux. Le Monde Informatique, 27 November 2012. Reports the cost comparison published by the city of Munich for the migration of about 11'000 users: the migration to LiMux and OpenOffice cost 22.8 million EUR, a migration to Windows 7 and Office 2010 would have cost a little over 34 million EUR and one to Windows 7 and OpenOffice 29.9 million EUR; LiMux saved 6.8 million EUR of software licences compared to Microsoft Office on Windows 7 and 4.7 million EUR of hardware upgrades, because LiMux runs on the existing hardware. A study of HP for Microsoft disputed the savings but was never published.

source_name: Schleswig-Holstein (2025) Digitale Souveränität ist möglich und wirtschaftlich
description: State government of Schleswig-Holstein, Ministry of Digitalisation (2025): Digitale Souveränität ist möglich und wirtschaftlich, 4 December 2025. The switch to open-source software saves more than 15 million EUR of licence costs, against nine million EUR of one-time investments planned for 2026 for the migration and the development of the open-source solutions; nearly 80 percent of all workplaces outside the tax administration use LibreOffice. heise online (7 December 2025) reports the 15 million EUR as the saving of 2026 alone, with similar amounts in the following years.

source_name: Blind et al. (2021) The impact of Open Source Software and Hardware on the EU economy
description: Blind, K., Böhm, M., Grzegorzewska, P., Katz, A., Muto, S., Pätsch, S., Schubert, T. (2021): The impact of Open Source Software and Hardware on technological independence, competitiveness and innovation in the EU economy. Final study report for the European Commission, DG CONNECT. Companies located in the EU invested around 1 billion EUR in open-source software in 2018, which resulted in an impact on the European economy of between 65 and 95 billion EUR; the cost-benefit ratio is above 1:4; an increase of 10 percent of the open-source contributions would annually generate an additional 0.4 to 0.6 percent GDP and more than 600 additional ICT start-ups; by procuring open-source instead of proprietary software the public sector could reduce the total cost of ownership and avoid vendor lock-in.

source_name: Hoffmann, Nagle & Zhou (2024) The Value of Open Source Software
description: Hoffmann, M., Nagle, F., Zhou, Y. (2024): The Value of Open Source Software. Harvard Business School Strategy Unit Working Paper 24-038, not peer reviewed. Based on the Census II of free and open source software and BuiltWith: the supply-side value, the cost to recreate the most widely used open-source software once, is 4.15 billion USD, while the demand-side value, the cost if every firm had to rebuild the open-source software it uses, is 8.8 trillion USD; firms would need to spend 3.5 times more on software than they currently do if open-source software did not exist.

Greenstein, S., Nagle, F. (2014): Digital dark matter and the economic contribution of Apache. Research Policy 43(4), 623-631. Based on a 1 percent sample of all outward-facing web servers in the United States, the use of Apache potentially accounts for a mismeasurement of somewhere between 2 and 12 billion USD, between 1.3 and 8.7 percent of the stock of prepackaged software in the private fixed investment of the United States.

source_name: Nagle (2019) Open Source Software and Firm Productivity
description: Nagle, F. (2019): Open Source Software and Firm Productivity. Management Science 65(3), 1191-1215. Free open-source software has a positive and significant value-added return for firms with an ecosystem of complementary capabilities and none for firms without it; for these firms a 1 percent increase in the use of free open-source software leads to an increase of the value-added productivity of between 0.002 and 0.008 percent; the effect is smaller for larger firms.

source_name: CSRB (2024) Review of the Summer 2023 Microsoft Exchange Online Intrusion
description: Cyber Safety Review Board (2024): Review of the Summer 2023 Microsoft Exchange Online Intrusion, 20 March 2024. The threat actor Storm-0558 compromised the Microsoft Exchange Online mailboxes of 22 enterprise organizations and 503 related personal accounts worldwide and downloaded approximately 60'000 emails from the US State Department alone; the intrusion was preventable and succeeded because of a cascade of security failures at Microsoft, whose security culture was inadequate and requires an overhaul.

source_name: Parametrix (2024) CrowdStrike's impact on the Fortune 500
description: Parametrix (2024): CrowdStrike's impact on the Fortune 500. The total direct financial loss facing the US Fortune 500 companies, excluding Microsoft, from the CrowdStrike outage of 19 July 2024 is 5.4 billion USD.

Chancel, L., Piketty, T., Saez, E., Zucman, G. et al. (2022): World Inequality Report 2022, World Inequality Lab, executive summary: the richest 10 percent of the global population own 76 percent of all wealth and the poorest half 2 percent; the richest 10 percent take 52 percent of the global income and the poorest half 8.5 percent; the top 1 percent took 38 percent of all additional wealth accumulated since the mid-1990s; the share of the global wealth of the billionaires rose from 1 percent in 1995 to over 3 percent; the wealth of the richest individuals grew at 6 to 9 percent per year since 1995, the average wealth at 3.2 percent per year.

source_name: OECD (2014) Focus on Inequality and Growth
description: OECD (2014): Focus on Inequality and Growth, December 2014, contact Federico Cingano, summary of Cingano, F. (2014): Trends in Income Inequality and its Impact on Economic Growth, OECD Social, Employment and Migration Working Papers No. 163, DOI 10.1787/5jxrjncwxv6j-en. A rise of the income inequality by 3 Gini points, the average increase in the OECD over the past two decades, drags down the economic growth by 0.35 percentage point per year for 25 years, a cumulated loss of the GDP of 8.5 percent at the end of the period; the rise of the inequality 1985-2005 knocked more than 10 percentage points off the cumulative growth 1990-2010 of the GDP per capita in Mexico and New Zealand, nearly 9 points in the United Kingdom, Finland and Norway and between 6 and 7 points in the United States, Italy and Sweden; the gap between the bottom four deciles and the rest drives the effect, no evidence is found that the pulling away of the high incomes harms growth; a 6 points higher income inequality (the US-Canada difference in 2010) lowers the numeracy of the individuals with a low parental education background by around 6 points, nearly 40 percent of the gap to the medium background.

Ostry, J. D., Berg, A., Tsangarides, C. G. (2014): Redistribution, Inequality, and Growth. IMF Staff Discussion Note SDN/14/02. An increase of the net Gini from 37 (the United States in 2005) to 42 (Gabon in 2005) decreases the growth on average by 0.5 percentage points, from 5 to 4.5 percent per year, holding the redistribution and the initial income constant; a one-Gini-point increase of the inequality is associated with a 6 percentage point higher risk that a growth spell ends the next year, i.e. a decrease of the expected spell length of about 7 percent; the redistribution itself does not lower the growth unless it is already very high.

Zucman, G. (2013): The Missing Wealth of Nations: Are Europe and the U.S. net Debtors or net Creditors? Quarterly Journal of Economics 128(3), 1321-1364. Abstract: around 8 percent of the global financial wealth of the households is held in tax havens, three-quarters of which goes unrecorded.

Alstadsæter, A., Johannesen, N., Zucman, G. (2019): Tax Evasion and Inequality. American Economic Review 109(6), 2073-2103. Leaked customer lists of offshore financial institutions matched to the administrative wealth records of Norway, Sweden and Denmark: the offshore tax evasion is highly concentrated among the rich; the 0.01 percent richest households evade about 25 percent of their taxes, while the tax evasion detected in stratified random tax audits is less than 5 percent throughout the distribution.

source_name: EU Tax Observatory (2023) Global Tax Evasion Report 2024
description: Alstadsæter, A., Godar, S., Nicolaides, P., Zucman, G. (2023): Global Tax Evasion Report 2024, EU Tax Observatory, October 2023. USD 12 trillion, the equivalent of 12 percent of the world GDP, was held offshore by households at the end of 2022 (financial assets only, reported and unreported); thanks to the automatic exchange of bank information the offshore tax evasion has declined by a factor of about three in less than 10 years and in the central scenario only about 25 percent of the offshore wealth evades taxation; the global billionaires have effective personal tax rates equivalent to 0 to 0.5 percent of their wealth, closer to 0.5 percent in the United States and closer to 0 percent in France; the wealth of the global billionaires has grown at 7 percent a year on average since 1995 net of inflation; a minimum tax of 2 percent of the wealth of the about 2'500 billionaires with close to USD 13 trillion would raise nearly USD 250 billion per year.

Gilens, M., Page, B. I. (2014): Testing Theories of American Politics: Elites, Interest Groups, and Average Citizens. Perspectives on Politics 12(3), 564-581. 1'779 policy issues of the United States: the economic elites and the organised business groups have substantial independent impacts on the policy, while the average citizens and the mass-based interest groups have little or no independent influence; in the multivariate model 4 the logit coefficient of the preferences of the economic elites (90th income percentile) is 0.76 and the one of the average citizens (50th income percentile) is 0.03 and not significant. The coefficients are taken from the reprint of the table in Bashir, O. S. (2015): Testing Inferences about American Politics: A Review of the 'Oligarchy' Result, Research and Politics, DOI 10.1177/2053168015608896, who argues that the high correlation of the two preferences makes the near-zero coefficient of the average citizens too likely to be produced by chance.

Corak, M. (2013): Income Inequality, Equality of Opportunity, and Intergenerational Mobility. Journal of Economic Perspectives 27(3), 79-102. The Great Gatsby Curve: the countries with more inequality also have less earnings mobility across the generations; in Finland, Norway and Denmark less than one-fifth of any economic advantage or disadvantage of a father is passed on to his son, in Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States roughly 50 percent; the American intergenerational earnings elasticity at about 0.5 is twice as high as the Canadian; the curve is a correlation, not a causal estimate.

Kondo, N., Sembajwe, G., Kawachi, I., van Dam, R. M., Subramanian, S. V., Yamagata, Z. (2009): Income inequality, mortality, and self rated health: meta-analysis of multilevel studies. BMJ 339, b4471. The cohort relative risk of mortality per 0.05 unit increase of the Gini coefficient is 1.08 (95 percent confidence interval 1.06 to 1.10), stronger above a Gini of 0.3; if the relation is causal, upwards of 1.5 million deaths or 9.6 percent of the adult mortality could be averted in 30 OECD countries by levelling the Gini coefficient below 0.3; the excess risks are 3 percent in Japan, 11 percent in the United States and 38 percent in Mexico.

Taneja, A., Kamande, A., Guharay Gomez, C., Abed, D., Lawson, M., Mukhia, N. (2025): Takers not Makers: The unjust poverty and unearned wealth of colonialism. Oxfam International, 20 January 2025, an advocacy report based on the Forbes billionaire estimates: the billionaire wealth rose three times faster in 2024 than in 2023, by USD 2 trillion to USD 15 trillion with 2'769 billionaires (the amounts as reported by Al Jazeera on 20 January 2025); 60 percent of the billionaire wealth comes from inheritance, cronyism and corruption or monopoly power.

Kleinertz B., Pellinger C., von Roon S., Hübner T. (FfE Research Center for Energy Economics), Kaestle G.: EU Displacement Mix - A Simplified Marginal Method to Determine Environmental Factors for Technologies Coupling Heat and Power in the European Union. Final report for COGEN Europe, Munich, May 2018, ISBN 978-3-941802-39-1. Key finding (executive summary): the marginal CO2 equivalent emission factor of the EU-28 displacement mix incl. the upstream chain and 5 percent grid losses is 986 g CO2/kWh excluding nuclear power plants and 446 g CO2/kWh if nuclear power plants are included as must-run; generation shares from the Eurostat data of 2015.

Ramseier L., Frischknecht R. (treeze Ltd.): Umweltkennwerte und Primärenergiefaktoren von Energiesystemen, UVEK Ökobilanzdatenbestand DQRv2:2022, for KBOB, BAFU and AHB, Uster, 9 March 2022. Table 'Elektrizität, Bezug via Netz' gives the greenhouse gas emissions per MJ of electricity for the Swiss mixes of 2018 (CH-Verbrauchermix 0.035, CH-Produktionsmix 0.009, CH-Lieferantenmix HKN 0.015 kg CO2-eq/MJ) and for photovoltaic electricity (Fotovoltaik 0.013 kg CO2-eq/MJ); the mixes are documented in Krebs & Frischknecht (2020) and Frischknecht et al. (2020), Umweltbilanz Strommixe Schweiz 2018, BAFU.

Krebs L., Frischknecht R. (treeze Ltd.): Umweltbilanz Strommixe Schweiz 2018, v2.01, for the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN/BAFU), Uster, 27 April 2021. The life cycle inventories of the Swiss production mix, the supplier mix based on guarantees of origin (HKN, 54.7 g CO2-eq/kWh) and the consumption mix of 2018.
